entities.name: Notre-Dame de la Garde
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Notre-Dame de la Garde ('Our Lady of the Watchtower'), the Romano-Byzantine basilica crowning the highest point in Marseille at 162 meters above sea level, completed in 1864 under Napoleon III, is the most beloved building in Marseille and the city's most visible landmark — watched over by a 9.7-meter gilded bronze statue of the Virgin Mary that has guided sailors since the chapel's founding in 1214. The basilica is known by Marseillais as 'La Bonne Mère' (the Good Mother) and remains one of France's most visited pilgrimage sites.

A chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary has stood on the Garde hill since 1214, when a monk named Pierre obtained permission to build an oratory. The current Neo-Byzantine basilica was designed by architect Henri-Jacques Espérandieu and built 1853-1864, replacing an earlier medieval chapel. The site served as a Royalist and later Vichy stronghold during WWII, and bullet holes from the 1944 Liberation of Marseille are preserved in the basilica's interior walls as deliberate memorials.

The basilica's interior is decorated with thousands of ex-votos (votive offerings) — small paintings, model ships, photographs, and plaques placed by sailors, fishermen, and pilgrims who survived danger or received answered prayers. The collection of over 5,000 ex-votos represents one of the most remarkable records of popular devotion in France. The gilded Virgin atop the bell tower is visible from 50 kilometers at sea — her most ancient function as maritime landmark preserved in her name.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Notre-Dame de la Garde's 800-year continuity as maritime landmark, its 5,000 ex-votos recording popular devotion, and its preserved Liberation bullet holes make it the building that most completely encodes Marseille's identity as Mediterranean port city and wartime resistance survivor.
